source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — flamingo
facts: Flamingos filter food while holding their bills upside down in the water.
A flamingo's bill contains tiny filtering plates that trap food as water flows out.
Flamingos build raised mud nests to help protect their eggs from flooding.
Both male and female flamingos can feed chicks a milk-like digestive secretion.
Flamingo parents can lose some of their bright colour while feeding young.
Flamingo parents recognise their own chicks by their calls in crowded colonies.
Flamingo chicks gather in nursery groups watched by adults.
Some flamingos feed in salty or caustic lakes that few other animals tolerate.
Flamingos often take a running start into the wind to get airborne.
Courting flamingos can march in tightly packed groups, abruptly changing direction together.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — ostrich
facts: Ostriches do not bury their heads in sand when frightened.
An ostrich has only two toes on each foot.
Ostriches use their wings for balance during sharp turns even though they cannot fly.
Ostriches swallow small stones to help grind food inside their bodies.
Several female ostriches can lay eggs in one communal nest.
Male ostriches generally take the night shift when incubating eggs.
Ostriches can shelter their chicks beneath their wings from sun and rain.
An ostrich can sprint at around 70 kilometres per hour.
Ostrich feathers lack the tightly interlocking structure of many flying birds' feathers.
An ostrich egg is enormous, but small compared with the size of the bird laying it.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — kiwi
facts: A kiwi has nostrils near the tip of its long bill, useful for locating food.
Kiwis have tiny wings hidden beneath their feathers.
Kiwi feathers are loose and hair-like rather than forming a smooth flying surface.
Kiwis have whisker-like feathers around the face.
A kiwi lays an egg that can weigh about a fifth of its own body weight.
Kiwi chicks emerge with substantial yolk reserves to fuel their first days.
Unlike many birds, kiwis have heavy bones filled with marrow.
Kiwis can sneeze dirt out of the nostrils at their bill tips.
Kiwis use underground burrows as shelter.
Genetic evidence links kiwis closely to Madagascar's extinct elephant birds.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — hornbill
facts: A hornbill's long eyelashes are modified feathers.
Many hornbills seal their nesting female inside a tree cavity, leaving a feeding slit.
Male hornbills deliver food through the narrow opening of a sealed nest.
Some hornbill chicks reseal their cavity after their mother leaves.
Ground hornbills do not follow the sealed-nest routine of many tree-dwelling relatives.
Yellow-billed hornbills forage alongside dwarf mongooses, benefiting from insects the mammals disturb.
The helmeted hornbill has a dense casque, unlike the mostly hollow structures of other hornbills.
Some male hornbills collide their casques in mid-flight contests.
Some nesting female hornbills shed flight feathers while safely enclosed in their cavities.
Ground hornbills can use their long bills like tongs when handling dangerous prey.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — owl
facts: An owl's facial disc channels sound toward its ear openings.
Owls turn their heads to look around because their eyes cannot swivel like ours.
Owls can turn their heads roughly three-quarters of a circle, not a full revolution.
Soft feather edges help many owls fly with very little noise.
Owls regurgitate pellets containing bones and hair they cannot digest.
Not all owls hunt at night; some are active in daylight.
Many owls reuse abandoned nests instead of constructing their own.
Burrowing owls use underground burrows as homes.
Barn owls have heart-shaped facial discs.
Owls sharing a region can reduce competition by hunting different prey or at different times.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — cassowary
facts: Cassowary feathers look almost like coarse black hair.
A cassowary's helmet has a spongy interior beneath a keratin covering.
Female cassowaries are generally larger than males.
Cassowaries produce deep booming calls that can carry through dense forest.
A cassowary has a long, dagger-like claw on each inner toe.
Cassowaries can swim despite being large, flightless forest birds.
Cassowaries spread large rainforest seeds in their droppings.
Some rainforest seeds germinate better after passing through a cassowary.
The dwarf cassowary lacks the dangling neck wattles of its larger relatives.
Cassowary plumage helps protect against rainforest thorns rather than powering flight.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — secretary bird
facts: Secretary birds are birds of prey that usually hunt on foot.
A secretary bird can kill prey with powerful stamping kicks.
Secretary birds can fly well despite spending much of the day walking.
Secretary birds roost and nest high in trees.
A secretary bird can cover more than thirty kilometres during a day's hunt.
Secretary birds carry food in their bills rather than grasping it with their feet.
Secretary birds may search recently burned ground for exposed prey.
Pairs of secretary birds can reuse the same large nest for years.
Secretary bird parents feed their chicks regurgitated food.
Secretary bird courtship can involve circling, swooping flights high above their walking territory.
